summary.text: The Lorentz force is the push a charged particle feels from electric and magnetic fields.
The electric part speeds the particle up along a straight line, while the magnetic part acts sideways to both its motion and the field and bends its path.
Together with Maxwell's equations it underpins classical electrodynamics, from electric motors and particle accelerators to plasmas.

facts.label: Who derived it
facts.value: Hendrik Lorentz gave a complete derivation in 1895

facts.label: Heaviside's part
facts.value: Oliver Heaviside found the magnetic part a few years before

facts.label: Right-hand rule
facts.value: Velocity, field and force directions fit index finger, middle finger, thumb

facts.label: Path in uniform field
facts.value: Circular or helical, known as cyclotron motion

facts.label: Where it fails
facts.value: At small scales where quantum effects, like spin, matter

items.prompt: An electron flies straight into a region with a steady magnetic field pointing sideways to its motion. How does its path change?

options.label: It speeds up in a straight line
It bends along a curve
It stops dead at the edge
It continues unchanged

items.explain: The magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity and field, so it curves the particle's path, often into a circle or helix.

items.prompt: A designer wants to increase a particle's speed along a straight line. Which part of the Lorentz force does that job?

options.label: The magnetic part, because it pushes along the motion
Neither part, since forces cannot change speed
The electric part, which pushes along the field
Both equally, because they always point the same way

items.explain: Only the electric field can transfer energy to or from a particle. The magnetic force is sideways to the velocity and does no work.

items.prompt: Why can a magnetic field steer a moving particle in circles without ever making it faster?

options.label: Its force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work
Its force is always zero once the particle moves
It converts the particle's mass into speed and back
It pushes straight forward, then straight backward

items.explain: The magnetic term vanishes in the power calculation because a vector is always perpendicular to its cross product with another vector.

items.prompt: A wire carrying a steady current sits in an external magnetic field. What happens to the wire as a whole?

options.label: Nothing, since the wire itself is neutral
Its moving charges each feel the force, so it feels one net push
Only the current is affected, never the wire
The field stops the charges, so the current dies

items.explain: Each moving charge in the wire experiences the Lorentz force, and together these forces produce a net macroscopic force on the wire.

items.prompt: Some textbooks start from the force law itself to say what the electric and magnetic fields are. What do they take the fields to be?

options.label: Whatever the force on a charge of known velocity would be there
Only the push felt by charges that are currently present
The energy a charge has stored inside the field
The speed a charge reaches after leaving the region

items.explain: The fields E and B are defined at each point by the force a hypothetical charged particle with a given velocity would experience there, even if no charge is present.

items.prompt: A physicist wants to know whether the Lorentz force law is the final word on tiny particles. What is the honest answer?

options.label: It is exact at every scale, including quantum ones
It fails at small scales, where spin adds interactions it ignores
It fails only for particles moving slowly
It was disproved once special relativity appeared

items.explain: The law remains valid in special relativity but breaks down at small scales where quantum effects matter, such as spin interactions it does not include.
